stories.headline: Update: Houthi Missile Strike on Yemeni Training Camp Kills 73 Security Recruits
stories.summary:
A Houthi ballistic missile strike on a security training camp in Yemen's central Shabwa province has killed 73 people, local authorities said Tuesday, making it the deadliest reported attack since the current escalation began. The Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group fired three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city on Monday. The site, the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, was being used to train recruits for the internal security forces and police.

Shabwa's media office initially reported 53 dead and 200 wounded, but said in a new statement that an investigative committee had raised the death toll to 73, with another 14 people missing. Hospitals were overwhelmed, and the most seriously wounded were moved to Hadramout and Aden, according to deputy governor Fahad al-Khalifi. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani called the attack a war crime, arguing the facility was not a military target. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council, condemned a "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response."

The Houthis' military spokesman said the group had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations." Yemen's civil war has flared in recent months. Pro-government forces launched a major offensive at the start of October, backed by Saudi-led coalition air support, and retook Red Sea coastal territory overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait that the Houthis seized in September. Heavy fighting continues there, around besieged Taiz, and in Marib and al-Jawf provinces, while the Houthis have fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases.

stories.headline: Pope Leo Returns to St. Peter's Square for First Audience Since Cancer Surgery
stories.summary:
Pope Leo returned to St. Peter's Square on Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from an open-air popemobile as he held his first general audience since lung cancer surgery eight days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on October 13 and has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. It was his first audience since October 7.

Leo opened the 50-minute event by thanking the crowd for "the support and prayers," without directly mentioning his health, and spoke in a clear voice. He delivered a sermon in Italian and, in the only notable change from past audiences, offered brief greetings in seven languages rather than nine. Crowds gathered hours ahead in drizzling weather.

Doctors have said the surgery was completed without complications, but they have not disclosed the tumor's size or whether the disease spread to nearby lymph nodes, both key to prognosis. The Vatican has given no schedule beyond Wednesday. The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, and it remains unclear whether the trip will proceed as planned. His lead surgeon has said he could be fully recovered in time, while the Vatican's secretary of state has suggested the pace of his schedule may need to be adjusted. Leo, elected in May 2025, leads the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

stories.headline: Update: Trump and Zelensky at Odds Despite Oslo Talks as Rift Deepens
stories.summary:
A BBC analysis finds that the relationship between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has reached one of its lowest points, even as US envoy Steve Witkoff embraced Zelensky before talks in Oslo. Zelensky posted video of the moment with the message "Ukraine is working for peace," but analysts doubt it dispels his misgivings about US policy.

Trump told Newsmax last week that "Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," and on Monday said "Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about" when asked about the Ukrainian leader's claim that a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Zelensky, usually circumspect, told a US congressional delegation of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced fear that a political decision had been made to slow support. On Telegram Monday he wrote that Kyiv has welcomed "literally EVERY attempt" to end the war with dignity, rebutting Trump's charge that he is the main obstacle to a settlement.

The article notes earlier ruptures, including the February 2025 Oval Office clash that led to a week-long suspension of aid, were followed by reversals, and that Trump has swung sharply on other leaders such as Israel's Netanyahu. Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform said Trump can always U-turn but that "this does look bad." Supply of US-made Patriot air defence missiles has slowed to a trickle after this year's US war with Iran and a global shortage.

stories.headline: Update: France Divided Over Who Is to Blame for Riots as Parliamentary Inquiry Proposed
stories.summary:
France remains split over who orchestrated the October 17 riots and what lessons to draw. National Assembly president Yael Braun-Pivet has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised. Reports say more than 3,000 shops and businesses were looted, much of it apparently opportunistic, with some looters trying to sell stolen goods online.

French intelligence had told government circles that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in student protests, and a circled capital A was spray-painted on buildings nationwide. Le Figaro published a September 29 intelligence report alleging student unions and radical-left movements manipulated demonstrations, and suggesting the party La France Insoumise was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential election. LFI denies this.

President Emmanuel Macron, viewed by many as a lame duck, and his government are accused of failing to keep the country safe. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice, and online sales platforms say they will help authorities track looters. Police are examining CCTV and social media footage. Some Parisians told the BBC the violence does not represent France and rejected talk of civil war.

stories.headline: Update: Fox News Investigation Finds 101 Groups Across 13 Countries Behind New Rounds of French Protests
stories.summary:
Two days after an estimated 500,000 demonstrators poured into streets across France and clashes left parts of Paris and other cities burning, activists are calling supporters back out on Saturday, Oct. 24, for a second protest billed as "Acte II." A digital map of the plans lists 212 "mobilizations." A separate call has gone out for a coordinated European youth strike on Friday, Nov. 20.

A Fox News Digital investigation says it has identified 101 organizations in 13 countries, including the United States, that are coordinating, organizing or amplifying the protests, up from 54 identified on Monday. According to the report, most of the groups are adult-led, and 33 are led by students or youth. Fox describes the network as a "red-green" alliance of Islamist organizations and far-left, communist and socialist groups, and says some groups use the "Antifa" label. It also cites U.S. academic Hatem Bazian, founder of Students for Justice in Palestine and American Muslims for Palestine, for sharing videos of the protests. Bazian did not respond to a request for comment.

The findings reflect the right-leaning framing of the unrest, which stresses organized, ideologically driven coordination. French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the unrest is being exploited, and he has acknowledged intelligence failures. Critics on the left and many protesters present the demonstrations as a response to broader grievances, including conditions in French schools and wider social frustrations, rather than as a centrally directed campaign. The Fox report's characterization of the groups has not been independently verified in the material provided.

The next test comes Saturday, when authorities must decide how to handle the planned Acte II events. Several French cities have already extended curfews, and about 1,800 people were arrested in earlier violence.

stories.headline: Update: Musk Ordered Starshield Slowdown That Hampered Ukraine, Wall Street Journal Reports
stories.summary:
Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink satellite internet, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter. Ukraine has said the disruption hampered its ability to respond to Russian attacks. The slowdown reportedly affected Ukrainian drones, airplanes and helicopters.

CBS News, citing its own sources, reported that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, and that he chose to limit access in ways that affected drone operations. The reports come as Musk and President Donald Trump have both recently criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has also flagged disruptions in U.S. intelligence sharing.

The revelation is notable because Starlink and Starshield have been central to Ukrainian battlefield communications, and a single executive's decision can affect military operations. It also arrives amid other Musk-related business news. He said on SpaceX's earnings call that special committees of independent directors at SpaceX and Tesla are examining a possible merger, which he called a good idea. SpaceX reported third-quarter net income of $4.4 billion, well above the average analyst estimate.

It was not clear from the available reporting whether Musk or SpaceX has responded publicly to the specific allegations. The matter is likely to draw scrutiny from lawmakers and Ukrainian officials over reliance on privately controlled infrastructure in wartime.

stories.headline: Trump and Vance Announce $25 Million Fraud Whistleblower Program
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25 million program to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the federal government. Qualifying tipsters would receive a 1% commission. The announcement was made alongside independent journalist Nick Shirley.

Separately, the Department of Homeland Security launched a nationwide ICE operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, resulting in multiple arrests, Fox News reported. Supporters of the administration's approach say it protects taxpayer money and rewards citizens who expose abuse. Critics of such efforts have often raised concerns about whether enforcement is targeted fairly and about the incentives created by commission-based tips, though the available coverage did not detail specific objections to this program.

At the same event, Trump said it was too early to think about endorsing a successor. Vance said he believes Trump would endorse him for 2028 but that they have not discussed a run. The program comes with midterm elections two weeks away and with fraud a prominent theme for the administration. Details on how the commission will be calculated and paid have yet to be fully spelled out in the reporting provided.

stories.headline: Update: Ramaswamy Campaign Spends $4 Million on Ad Featuring Rival Amy Acton's Estranged Mother
stories.summary:
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is putting $4 million behind an ad in which Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calls her daughter a "liar" and urges voters to reject her. Axios reported the buy, saying the campaign is doubling down despite bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy confirmed to reporters Tuesday that "it is an ad from our campaign."

In the spot, Arthur disputes Acton's account of her upbringing and her claims of childhood abuse. Acton has said her mother sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted her at age 12. Acton's brother called the ad a "despicable low" and said their stepfather abused Acton as a child. Acton accused Ramaswamy of a "lifelong pattern" of personal attacks.

Criticism has crossed party lines. Meghan McCain called it a "dastardly ad," and Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown demanded that Republican Sen. Jon Husted condemn it. Ramaswamy's campaign is gambling that the message will resonate with voters in a race NBC News describes as tightening in its final two weeks. Ramaswamy's allies have defended the ad as a legitimate challenge to Acton's personal narrative, while opponents call it exploitation of a family trauma.
